Agreed next steps: run benchmark, share updated cost spreadsheet, and reconvene after results.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-11 10:00 PDT | 46m | Attendees: Maya, Daniel (Redwood); Priya, Ethan, Sana (Aurora)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got about 45 minutes. quick agenda, cost review, benchmarks Daniel ran, tradeoffs, then next steps. Priya, you want to add anything?
00:14 Priya: nope that sounds good, mostly want to understand tokens per dollar and where we hit tails on latency. we run mixed traffic - short queries and some long product description generations.
00:30 Daniel: cool, so I ran the 30-minute microbench with the model variant you asked (redwood-v2-3b-qt) on a p4-like instance. raw numbers: baseline (no caching, small batch) ~ 1,200 tokens/sec at 95th percentile cost ~ $0.018 per 1k tokens. with prefix caching enabled for repeated prompts we saw tokens/sec jump to ~3,800 and effective cost drop to about $0.006 per 1k tokens.
01:05 Ethan: wait, is that tokens per second per GPU or overall?
01:08 Daniel: per GPU. the test used a single GPU instance. total throughput depends on cluster size. the important bit is relative improvement from caching.
01:20 Sana: i want to understand what 'prefix caching' means here, are we saving the full KV cache across requests?
01:27 Daniel: yes, so for repeated prefixes (like same product boilerplate) we store the KV cache and re-use it, avoids re-computing early layers. it behaves like a warm KV cache. sometimes the transcription tools say K V cache, but it's the same idea.
01:42 Priya: ok makes sense. how sensitive is that to prompt variability? our product text has some templating but also dynamic content.
01:50 Daniel: variability kills some savings; if the prefix diverges more than a few tokens the cache hit rate drops. in your sample traffic the hit-rate is about 42% for exact prefix reuse, but if we allow fuzzy prefix matching we can push to ~58% hits at the cost of extra bookkeeping.
02:12 Maya: real quick on pricing: hosted vs dedicated. our hosted SKU assumes multi-tenant and uses amortized GPU cost, so per-token price is lower for spiky workloads but you lose isolation guarantees. dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and slightly better unit economics at scale, but you need a commit.
02:33 Ethan: do you have an example calc for our qps? we estimate 120 qps average with spikes to 600 qps.
02:40 Daniel: yes — i ran a quick costing. with caching and moderate batching (batch window 30ms) on hosted, your effective tokens/sec/$ looked like ~2,500 tokens/sec per $1 for the reads-heavy flows. dedicated with a 6-month commit drops that to ~3,300 tokens/sec per $1 because of reserved pricing and more aggressive batching/kv tuning.
03:00 Priya: what's the impact on tail latency when you batch more aggressively? our product needs 95th < 500ms for short queries.
03:07 Daniel: so batching gives you throughput but increases p95 depending on configured window. with 30ms batch window we saw median 70ms and p95 ~300ms. with 80ms batching p95 moves to ~640ms which would break your SLO. also caching helps reduce effective latency for cached prefixes.
03:30 Sana: and quantization? we saw inaccuracies on some generated text when quantized models are used.
03:36 Daniel: quantization (4-bit/INT4) reduces memory and can increase throughput but may degrade output quality for some sensitive tasks. our recommendation: do quantization for lower-priority endpoints (bulk tagging) and keep full precision for critical generation. we can also use mixed-precision where inner layers are full precision and outer layers quantized. results vary with the model family.
04:00 Priya: can you explain the tokens/sec/$ metric again? how should we interpret it?
04:05 Maya: tokens/sec per dollar is a quick way to compare throughput across config. basically higher means more tokens you can generate per unit spend; for latency-sensitive endpoints you weight p95 as a constraint and may accept lower tokens/sec/$ to meet latency.
04:22 Priya: our primary KPI is user perceived latency, but cost is also material. CFO would want cost per 1M tokens monthly.
04:30 Maya: understood, so we'll provide both — tokens/sec/$ and $ per 1M tokens and the latency tradeoffs for each config.
04:40 Ethan: you mentioned caching gave ~3x improvement. is that realistic across our suite?
04:45 Daniel: depends on reuse. for pure conversational flows with high prefix reuse we saw 4x. For product descr flows with moderate reuse more like 2.5-3x. your mixed traffic likely lands in that mid-range. i included hit-rate breakdown in the shared spreadsheet.
05:05 Priya: the spreadsheet had some assumptions, i want to validate them: average sequence length for short queries was 64 tokens and for long ops ~900 tokens?
05:14 Daniel: yes, that's from your sample corpus. we also simulated tail long-prompt bursts which drove KV cache warmups.
05:22 Sana: operational question — for dedicated can we control kernel selection/quantization flags? we need to run a few A/Bs.
05:28 Maya: yes, dedicated gives you more knobs; you can pin model build, kernel choices and quantization profile per route. hosted gives sensible defaults but less per-tenant customization.
05:40 Ethan: what about security — KMS, logs? we have SOC2 and data residency constraints for EU customers.
05:46 Maya: we support customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated and audit logs across deployments. hosted also supports region pinning and encryption at rest, and we have SOC2 Type 2 attestation. we'll attach the security pack.
06:05 Priya: excellent. Back to benchmarks — can we run a 1-hour test with our real traffic shape? that would help finance and infra make decisions.
06:13 Daniel: absolutely, i can run a 1-hour run with replayed traffic on both hosted and dedicated configs, with caching on/off and two batching windows (30ms and 80ms). i'll collect tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and cost per 1M tokens.
06:27 Maya: timeline?
06:29 Daniel: i can start Friday and deliver results Monday EOD, so target 2026-08-13 for raw logs and 2026-08-14 for cleaned analysis.
06:38 Priya: that's tight but good. CFO follow-up: please include $ per 1M tokens and monthly forecast at our estimated 120 qps baseline and a 3x spike model.
06:50 Daniel: noted, i'll include multi-scenarios: baseline, 2x, and 5x.
07:00 Sana: any caveats about caching skewing the fairness of the benchmark?
07:04 Daniel: yes, benchmarks must match production cache warming patterns; a synthetic uniform replay will overestimate hit rates. we'll do two runs: cold-start replay and warmed-run that replays realistic session sequences preserving user id grouping so prefixes warm naturally.
07:22 Priya: good. on the pricing deck side, can you put a line item for incremental engineering to implement fuzzy prefix matching? we might want that to increase cache hits.
07:32 Maya: we can estimate implementation effort; rough ballpark 2 engineer-weeks for fuzzy prefix matching integration plus monitoring. i'll note that as an optional line in the cost model.
07:45 Ethan: curious about autoscaling for dedicated — how fast can we spin up burst nodes? we can't afford long cold periods for Black Friday like spikes.
07:53 Daniel: dedicated supports burst capacity; typical spin-up is a few minutes if capacity is available, and we can do warm standby. for true instant elasticity you'd lean hosted for bursty peaks.
08:10 Priya: got it. any outstanding blockers?
08:13 Maya: looks like main blocker is running the 1-hour realistic benchmark and verifying hit-rate assumptions. also Priya to share the detailed traffic histogram.
08:22 Priya: i'll share that today.
08:24 Maya: ok, recap of next steps: Daniel run 1-hour benchmark (cold + warm) and share logs by 8/13; Maya to send updated pricing and the fuzzy-match engineering estimate by 8/12; Priya to share traffic shape by EOD; reconvene after we have the benchmark to decide hosted vs dedicated for pilot.
08:45 Sana: thanks all, this was helpful.
08:48 Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links to sheets and the security docs.
08:55 End of transcript

Notes: Some transcription artifacts present (K V cache vs KV cache, speaker overlaps). Shared artifacts referenced during call: cost-model-spreadsheet.xlsx (link in chat), security-pack.pdf (link), benchmark-run-templates (folder).
